title: Report on Studying at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich
paragraphs: I chose Germany as my destination because I myself had long had a strong interest in this country. I had heard that Germans have a national character similar to the Japanese, and I was interested in the path of Germany, which, like Japan, experienced defeat in war yet achieved great economic growth and became the largest economy in the EU, as well as in postwar Germany's view of history and its education, including the problem of Nazism. So I wanted, through studying abroad, not only to learn medicine but to experience German culture, people and history. In Nagoya University's clinical exchange, the German universities were Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (hereafter LMU), where I studied, and the University of Freiburg. I chose LMU because I could select neurology and oncology, my preferred specialties, at LMU. Also, the nature of the program, which guarantees many environments for students to get to know each other, was very attractive. Looking back now, the six weeks I spent in Munich were very fulfilling, a luxurious environment that responded to my goals to the fullest, and I am once again full of gratitude.

LMU holds a short-term clinical clerkship course called the Winter School every year, and LMU students and international students from around the world (this year from Brazil, Colombia, Georgia, Italy and Japan (Nagoya University, Yokohama National University and The Jikei University School of Medicine)) can take part in this course. The Winter School runs two courses, Oncology and Neurology, at the same time, and consists of each course's weekday curriculum and a joint program for both courses that includes weekend trips around Munich. I took part in the Oncology Winter School for four weeks, March 3 to 27. Ten international students and ten LMU students each took part in the Oncology Winter School, and we were able to interact deeply through lectures, weekend trips and life in the dormitory. On weekday mornings I was allowed to do procedures such as rounds, blood sampling and ECG measurement on the ward, and in the afternoon one to three lectures of 60 to 90 minutes were held daily. On the ward I worked in pairs with an LMU student (third to fifth year) as my Buddy. Conversations with patients and handovers between doctors during rounds were in German, so the Buddy translated as needed. The Buddy also taught me procedures. I cannot thank enough the Buddy who taught and helped me step by step. It was a good experience to be able to do many procedures that students do not do in Japan, and I was also very stimulated by the high level of the LMU students. On the ward, rounds were done on all patients every day, and it was impressive that every patient spoke a lot. I felt that most of the treatment was the same as in Japan, but there were also differences, such as performing bone marrow transplantation even in people in their 80s and different management criteria for transfusion (it seems there are differences in criteria between institutions in Japan too). In the afternoon lectures there were systematic lectures on cancer by organ, and I could also take lectures I had rarely taken in Japan, such as Psycho-Oncology and Palliative care, and learned a great deal. From March 31 to April 11, with only two Nagoya University students, I was allowed to take part in a neurology clerkship made possible by the efforts of Dr. Bustos of Nagoya University's International Collaboration Office and Dr. 勝野 of neurology. At German university hospitals it seems to be common for departments to be divided by disease, such as a stroke unit, an epilepsy unit and a neurodegenerative disease unit, and I was allowed to observe in a form of rotating through each unit. The doctors were very enthusiastic about teaching, letting me do neurological examinations of patients and carefully explaining in English each disease, pathology and the latest research, and I learned a great deal. I was also allowed to observe procedures such as EEG and EMG, and, when time allowed, the inpatient neurology ward, and I could see various diseases. Perhaps because it is a university hospital, it was impressive that biological tests were often performed locally. For the diagnosis of dementia, they of course did lumbar puncture to measure amyloid and tau, and I was surprised that amyloid PET and tau PET were also actively performed.

I also often heard about the healthcare situations and medical student life of various countries from the international students who had gathered not only from Germany but from around the world, including South America and Central Europe, which was very stimulating. In Germany and many other countries, medical students bear medical care as part of the workforce, and perhaps for that reason they seemed to me to be several steps ahead in both procedures and knowledge, and I was very stimulated. The Winter School itself also organised day bus trips on weekends, and it was very meaningful that we could all go not only to tourist spots such as Neuschwanstein Castle but also on social visits such as a guided tour of Dachau concentration camp. Also, in Munich, people under 30 can get the best seats at the Munich Philharmonic and the opera at the bargain price of 14 euros, and on Sundays the state art museums cost 1 euro, and I greatly enjoyed this luxurious artistic environment with friends. As I mentioned above, I was also interested in the history of Germany and Europe, so on weekends I took solo trips to Berlin and neighboring countries and visited museums, which is also a very impressive memory.

Thanks to the people and opportunities I was blessed with, I was able to have a truly wonderful experience on this study abroad. On the other hand, I also faced a major challenge myself. It was a strong sense of helplessness that, within the institution of a hospital, I was not at all useful to the people hosting me. I gained a lot of learning thanks to many people, but I felt frustrated and pathetic that, because of my lack of knowledge, experience and language ability, I could not repay them. In particular, although I knew that, since I was rotating in internal medicine, talking with patients in German was essential, I had somehow naively assumed that English alone would be enough, and I deeply reflected on that locally. Germans generally have high English ability, and there was no trouble at all with English at tourist spots, and moreover the English of the doctors and students was almost native level, so for expanding friendships as a student and receiving guidance from the doctors, there is no trouble with English alone. However, in order to "study abroad in Germany and live in Germany," or to "be useful on the ward and interact with patients," it was without doubt better to be able to speak German. I had never imagined that I would feel such a thick wall just from not being able to speak the language, and there were times I was quite depressed. Especially because Germany accepts many immigrants and faces the problems that come with it, a high level of German is required to work in Germany, and it was a society where "being able to speak German is taken for granted" more than I had expected. A doctor from Bosnia on my ward said that he had studied German so much that he had forgotten English. On the other hand, what I want to add is that most people understood that I could not speak German and helped me with halting English and various other means. As I mentioned above, Germans' general English ability is higher than that of the Japanese, so I even drank beer with a German sitting next to me at a restaurant in town, talking in English. So those who will study abroad from now on do not need to fear going to non-English-speaking countries excessively. What I want to convey is that "learning a language is a way of showing respect to the other person." My regret and reflection is that there might have been trust I could have built just by learning a few greetings and a few words. I think that by learning the language of the country, a more enjoyable life abroad awaits. My goal from now on is, I think, to return the kindness I received here to the many people I will meet. As a doctor, I will of course acquire and use specialised knowledge, but I strongly want to become a healthcare professional who is trusted by people of any background by consciously practising in daily life things that I noticed on this study abroad as "things that help when interacting with people from different communities": the ability to explain specialised knowledge to students and patients clearly in fluent English, learning at least a little of the other person's mother tongue when communicating with people from non-English-speaking backgrounds, and speaking first to people in trouble. Also, as a student aiming to become a hematologist, I was strongly struck by the words of an eminent leukemia authority in a lecture during this study abroad: "Anticancer drugs are poison. Medicine that uses such drugs must always be evidence-based." To do my best for patients, I want to be a healthcare professional who always learns eagerly as a scientist, takes on basic and clinical research too, and contributes even a little to the advancement of medicine. I aim to be a healthcare professional who always has a global perspective, does not fear challenges, and is active and needed in any environment.

Finally, I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to the professors of Nagoya University, beginning with Dr. 粕谷, Dr. 長谷川 and Dr. Bustos of the International Collaboration Office, who made this study abroad possible, the many doctors I met at LMU, my Buddy Andrea and my friends, the seniors who helped me prepare for studying abroad, my classmates who stimulated each other locally, and my family who always cheered me on. Thank you very much for making these irreplaceable six weeks possible.
